title: Singapore's Corporate Bond Market: Trends and Outlook
abstract: A quiet shift in Singapore's debt landscape is drawing attention from regional desks, with implications for issuers and investors alike.
body:
Singapore's corporate bond market has long been a steady, if unspectacular, corner of Asia's credit landscape. That characterisation is being tested in 2026. According to data compiled by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, gross Singapore dollar corporate bond issuance reached S$38.4 billion in the first four months of 2026, up 12.7 per cent from the same period a year earlier. The figure marks the strongest January-to-April total since 2021, when issuers rushed to lock in low rates before the global tightening cycle began.

The composition of that issuance has changed. Real estate developers, historically the largest borrowers in the local market, accounted for 28 per cent of new deals in the period, down from 41 per cent in 2020. Financial institutions and government-linked entities have filled the gap, together representing 47 per cent of volumes. Analysts at DBS Group Research note that the shift reflects both regulatory pressure on developers to deleverage and a broader demand from investors for shorter-dated, higher-rated paper.

## The rise of sustainability-linked structures

One of the more notable developments in 2026 has been the rapid adoption of sustainability-linked bond frameworks. In the first four months of the year, 19 Singapore dollar deals included a sustainability-linked component, compared with 11 in the whole of 2025. These structures tie the coupon to pre-defined environmental or social targets, typically stepping up by 25 to 50 basis points if the issuer misses its key performance indicators.

Not everyone is convinced. "The market is still figuring out how to price these deals," said Lim Wei Ling, head of Asian credit research at Maybank Securities, in an interview on 6 May 2026. "The step-up is often too small to change issuer behaviour, and the verification standards remain inconsistent across jurisdictions." Lim estimates that only about a third of sustainability-linked bonds issued in Singapore since 2023 have included third-party assurance on their targets.

Still, demand has been robust. A S$750 million 10-year sustainability-linked note from a Temasek-linked infrastructure firm priced in March 2026 at a spread of 68 basis points over the Singapore Overnight Rate Average, or SORA, with a book that was 3.2 times covered. Bankers involved in the deal said the order book included a significant number of European accounts, a rare occurrence for Singapore dollar paper.

## Foreign issuers return, cautiously

The Singapore dollar market has traditionally been a domestic affair, with foreign issuers accounting for less than 15 per cent of annual volumes. That share rose to 22 per cent in the first four months of 2026, the highest since 2019. The increase was driven largely by supranational and agency borrowers, including a S$1.2 billion five-year deal from the Asian Development Bank in February and a S$900 million three-year note from a European development bank in April.

Corporate foreign issuers remain scarce. Only two non-Singapore corporates priced Singapore dollar bonds in the period, both from Australian real estate trusts. The reluctance is partly a function of currency risk. The Singapore dollar has appreciated 3.4 per cent against the US dollar over the past twelve months, making unhedged borrowing more expensive for issuers whose revenues are in other currencies. Cross-currency basis swaps have also remained wide, adding to the cost.

"The economics work for supranationals because they have natural Singapore dollar needs or can swap at favourable terms," said Rajiv Menon, a rates strategist at CIMB Bank, on 28 April 2026. "For a typical European or American corporate, the all-in cost is still 30 to 40 basis points higher than in the euro or dollar market. That gap needs to narrow before we see a broader return."

## The Bank of Japan factor

A less obvious influence on Singapore's corporate bond market has been the policy stance of the Bank of Japan. As the BoJ has gradually normalised its yield curve control framework, Japanese investors have become more selective about foreign credit. Japan is a significant source of demand for Singapore dollar bonds, particularly at the longer end of the curve. Data from the Japan Securities Dealers Association show that Japanese investors were net sellers of foreign bonds in three of the first four months of 2026, a reversal from consistent net buying in 2024 and 2025.

Singapore issuers have felt the shift. A S$500 million 15-year deal from a local utility in January 2026 priced at 92 basis points over SORA, some 15 basis points wider than a comparable deal in November 2025. Bankers attributed the widening partly to reduced Japanese participation. "The marginal buyer has changed," said Menon. "Local insurers and asset managers are stepping in, but they are more price-sensitive and tend to prefer shorter tenors."

The BoJ's next policy meeting, scheduled for 17 June 2026, is widely expected to bring another modest increase in the policy rate. If that happens, Japanese demand for Singapore dollar credit could weaken further, at least in the near term. Some analysts see a silver lining. "Higher Japanese rates could eventually make the yen a more attractive funding currency again, which would help cross-currency swap levels," said Lim. "But that is a 2027 story, not a 2026 one."

## What to watch in the second half

The pipeline for the remainder of 2026 looks moderately busy. At least four Singapore real estate investment trusts have signalled plans to refinance existing debt in the third quarter, and two government-linked companies are expected to bring benchmark-sized deals. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has kept its Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate policy band unchanged at its April 2026 meeting, providing a stable backdrop for issuance.

The main risk is external. A sharper-than-expected slowdown in China, or a renewed spike in US Treasury yields, could compress demand for Asian credit more broadly. For now, however, the Singapore market appears to be weathering those cross-currents with its usual equanimity. Spreads on the iBoxx Singapore dollar corporate index stood at 78 basis points on 8 May 2026, 6 basis points tighter than at the start of the year. That is not a dramatic move, but in a market defined by stability, it counts as a vote of confidence.
